Pale Sun Inc. purchases 100% of Red Wash Mining, LLC from Northstar Minerals, Inc. on July 18, 2025. Henry Norwood is NMI's long-tenured owner/CEO and principal seller. Martin Shaw executes the Sable Harbor-side transaction. Mari owns the technical/operating assessment; Evan develops the platform and commercial case. None of these roles is substituted for another.

The acquisition does not sanitize East 12 continuity, variable metallurgy, tailings/water observations, closure omissions, maintenance backlog, fan/control redundancy, obsolete controls, assay/moisture timing, escalation errors, royalty step-up or title/easement defects. The [current casebook](../../red_wash/RED_WASH_CASEBOOK.md) and instruments preserve those items.

sections.heading: Closing consideration and accounting bridge
sections.text:
Operating assets $42.0M plus current assets $4.5M less ARO $16.0M and other assumed liabilities $2.5M equals $28.0M identifiable net assets and $28.0M cash consideration. Goodwill and transaction debt are zero in the selected case. The $3.0M environmental/title escrow and $0.5M holdback are portions of consideration, not additional purchase price: the reconstructed gross closing allocation is $24.5M direct seller payment + $3.0M escrow + $0.5M holdback = $28.0M.

The H2 2025 stabilization program is a separate $11.0M: $8.0M capitalized rehabilitation and $3.0M repair/stabilization expense. It must not be confused with ARU's later, separate $11.0M catch-up capital. The 2026 rehabilitation/sustaining budgets likewise follow the mine's source model rather than a duplicate acquisition-use line.

sections.heading: Instrument clauses and handover
sections.text:
The purchase instrument transfers the membership interests and preserves RWH as owner/operator. Disclosure schedules identify assumed liabilities and contract consent/notice status. Title/environmental claims use the dedicated Red Wash escrow; disputes do not permit silent netting against ARU's later escrow. The holdback is separately tracked against the identified transaction deliverables in the mine's instruments; this summary does not invent a released balance.

Operating authority passes to the buyer's retained mining organization at close. Norwood supplies records and transitional factual explanations without directing the mine. Cole remains site superintendent; Walt Sutter remains an external source. Hiring/retention and site-stop arrangements protect continuity without converting any person's memory into truth.

Selected resource, 2026 production, contracts and financial amounts reside in [RWH source](../../red_wash/source/core_operating_data.json). Their 2026 future periods retain forecast status. This historical close record does not claim that the entire 2026 plan was realized on July 18, 2025, or that the later ARU target was already a carrier/vendor.

sections.heading: Fred Tolman and the sellers
sections.text:
Fred Tolman, 65 in the derived 2026 biography, joined the predecessor logistics business in 1984 through commercial dispatch work. He learned terminal economics during the unsuccessful broad trucking venture, moved into general management as ARU formalized, assembled a controlling holding by 2002 and became CEO in 2006. He expanded repeat customers but deferred some asset renewal and never made succession fully independent of himself.

He sells because the next capital cycle and succession burden exceed what he wants to finance and lead. ARU is a viable going concern, not a rescue from insolvency. His knowledge remains useful after sale, while his authority ends at close. He is unrelated to Henry Norwood and is not the Red Wash seller.

The four sellers are Fred Tolman (60%), his sister Adele Tolman (20%), Nora Ashcombe (10%) and Seth Kettering (10%). All are synthetic U.S.-citizen natural persons holding one class of identical economic common shares. Adele is a passive family holder, not operating management. Nora and Seth sell every share and continue as employees without rollover. The [finance source](../source/finance.json) controls exact shares, proceeds and retention entries.

sections.heading: Origin of contact
sections.text: After the Q3 2025 external-carrier capacity change, Red Wash's Q4 carrier search broadened to rail/interface mapping. A documented October 17 inquiry identified ARU as BS&T's owner. Preliminary operating discussions on October 24 preceded acquisition interest. No banker introduced a ready-made Red Wash solution; no 2025 Red Wash movement or revenue is attributed to ARU/BS&T.

sections.heading: Reconstructed November 14 LOI terms
sections.text:
SHIH proposes a 100% ARU stock purchase at $62.0M enterprise value, subject to confirmatory diligence, a debt/cash/working-capital bridge and definitive documentation. The price assumes an independently viable $42.0M revenue/$9.8M normalized EBITDA business; it includes no Red Wash synergy guarantee. All minority shares participate. No earn-out and no seller rollover are contemplated.

The parties agree to a synthetic exclusivity period through December 19, with ordinary-course operation, access to books/assets/personnel under appropriate confidentiality, and no obligation to close until definitive conditions are met. The $11M catch-up need is disclosed as a buyer-funded stewardship program. It is separate from sustaining capex and the later mine-interface proposal.

Diligence conditions include the material customer renewal, collectible receivables, payroll and shared-service allocations, equipment/track condition, environmental reserve, open claim, lease/debt consents, four-person stock ownership, S eligibility and all-shareholder tax election cooperation. The railroad retains its corporate identity, common-carrier responsibilities and property-specific labor agreements.

The LOI directs the successor team to be interviewed before signing, because a nine-month seller consultancy cannot substitute for day-one management. Fred may explain relationships and history after close but cannot dispatch, hire, spend or direct employees. The final [approval and purchase-agreement summary](04_ARU_APPROVAL_AND_PURCHASE_AGREEMENT.md) records conditions actually adopted in the synthetic transaction.

The target is a capital-constrained, succession-thin logistics operator with a viable independent business. The principal question is whether its cash generation and local competence can survive an overdue capital cycle without acquisition-driven cost extraction. This memorandum retains management's representations separately from buyer conclusions.

sections.heading: Finding and evidence matrix
sections.text:
| Finding | Evidence available by December 15 | Management response and buyer disposition |
|---|---|---|
| Railroad's $1.5M EBITDA is below $2.05M sustaining capital | Traffic/expense, maintenance and sustaining schedules | Do not mistake consolidated margin for railroad profitability; value the full estate and fund identified assets |
| Nonrail margins require operating support | Contract/rate records, lease terms, labor and equipment allocations | Warehouse revenue includes contracted service/access charges; test shared-service allocation and occupancy rather than accept an EBITDA plug |
| Customer concentration and one material renewal | Customer/contract register with approximately 11% largest and 40% top five | Keep renewal sensitivity visible; no assumed post-cutoff renewal outcome |
| Track/drainage and locomotive backlog | Inspection findings and asset-level catch-up allocations | Authorize phased $11M equity-funded program; no undisclosed major bridge crisis or shutdown order is introduced |
| Known environmental obligation | Site records and reserve memorandum | Carry the derived $1.75M accrual; remediation/stormwater capex is not automatically an expense against that liability |
| Larger open claim | Claim chronology and counsel/insurer estimate | Carry $0.6M closing accrual with $0.7M possible adverse development; seller protects excess over accrual, subject to agreed recovery mechanics |
| Seller concentration of knowledge | Separate successor interviews and customer-handling walkthrough | Appoint Nora on day one; Fred's $225k consultancy supplies knowledge only |
| Labor and qualification | Property agreements and represented-craft register | SMART-TD train/engine and BMWED MOW continue; no assumption of national Class I terms |
| Tax eligibility | Four-person register, one economic share class, represented S history and BS&T QSub history | Obtain all seller signatures and separately document the tax assumptions; no government acceptance is invented |
| Red Wash interface | Independent 2025 books and preliminary customer requirements | Zero 2025 mine revenue; no automatic uranium custody; separate capital/rates decision |

The December 31 baseline and final generated 2025 statements are later artifacts. This December 15 memo records year-end expectations and available underlying contracts/condition evidence; it does not pretend the year had ended. The final baseline is available January 5 in the [chronology](../source/chronology.json). Exact model schedules are in [finance source](../source/finance.json).

sections.heading: Preserved investment disagreement
sections.text:
The buyer's financial reviewer argued that a 6.33× normalized EBITDA headline understated the $11M near-term capital burden and railroad renewal needs. The operating review agreed that the burden was real but argued it was finite and asset-specific, while the nonrail business retained customers and useful infrastructure. Neither side counted Red Wash as the answer. The board paper carries both views and the customer-loss/capital-overrun sensitivities.

Tessa objected to calling every owner-era cost an add-back. Only identified nonrecurring items survive the reported-to-normalized bridge. Nora objected to a broad centralization plan before the buyer understood local dispatch, working capital and customer interfaces. The adopted integration model protects those systems while improving evidence and succession.

sections.heading: Gate disposition
sections.text:
Proceed to signing only with the $4.5M working-capital peg and exclusions explicitly defined, debt/lease treatment reconciled, final disclosure schedules, employment/retention instruments, claim/environmental protections, financing commitments and operating authority clear. Any newly discovered shutdown condition or material unpriced structural defect returns the acquisition to the board; none is silently authored into the base case.

The existing CBAs and relevant regulatory responsibilities are obligations, not points awarded in an evaluation. The participant may challenge the valuation, the durability of nonrail margins or the adequacy of reserves. This record preserves the buyer's contemporary rationale without prescribing a hidden correct conclusion.

sections.heading: Buyer approval — December 17
sections.text:
The existing unitary board approves SHIH's acquisition of all ARU shares at $62M enterprise value, with the reconciled debt/cash bridge, $22.5M new term financing and $39M parent equity before fees. The derived $1.2M transaction/financing cash fees are incremental. A separate $11M equity-funded catch-up program is authorized by asset and timing, not added to purchase consideration or funded with extra acquisition debt.

The board considers the railway's thin post-maintenance cash contribution, nonrail contract margins, customer concentration, environmental/claim exposure and succession. It retains the dissent described in the [diligence memo](03_ARU_DILIGENCE_MEMORANDUM.md). Approval does not require a synergy quota, acquisition-driven headcount cuts or future Red Wash revenue. The reconstructed minute does not invent a unanimous roll-call or a new board/committee architecture.

sections.heading: Definitive agreement — December 19
sections.text:
**Parties and transfer.** Buyer is Sable Harbor Industrial Holdings, Inc.; target is American Resource Utility, Inc.; sellers are Fred Tolman, Adele Tolman, Nora Ashcombe and Seth Kettering. Every share transfers at the January 7 closing. There is no rollover, earn-out, statutory merger, or purchase of Red Wash in this instrument.

**Consideration.** Enterprise value is $62M. The debt/cash bridge produces $49.5M seller equity value before the $1.5M excess-cash distribution, leaving $48M buyer-funded consideration: $45M direct payment plus $3M escrow. The final bridge uses the source schedules; fees, retained leases and post-close capital are not counted again as seller proceeds.

**Working capital.** The derived peg is $4.5M, measured as eligible receivables + inventory + operating prepayments less trade payables and ordinary operating accruals. Cash, debt/finance leases, income taxes, environmental reserve and the separately scheduled larger claim are excluded to avoid double counting. Buyer submits the closing statement within 60 days; sellers have 30 days to object with line-level reasons; unresolved accounting disputes go to an independent accountant limited to disputed items. Adjustments are dollar-for-dollar.

**Representations and disclosure.** Sellers represent title to shares, capitalization, tax status, authority, financial records, identified contracts, labor arrangements, environmental matters, claims and disclosed assets. The information standard does not convert management forecasts into guaranteed results. Known defects stay in disclosure schedules and the operating model.

**Risk allocation.** General representations survive eighteen months, to July 7, 2027. The derived environmental survival period is five years, to January 7, 2031. The $3M escrow is part of ARU consideration and is separate from Red Wash's $3M escrow. Known environmental accrual is assumed; undisclosed environmental matters receive the extended seller protection. The larger identified claim has a $0.6M closing accrual and a specific seller indemnity for covered adverse development above that amount. Recovery cannot exceed actual covered loss and cannot be duplicated across insurance, escrow and seller recovery.

**Conduct and closing conditions.** ARU operates in the ordinary course until close. Closing requires stock-transfer documents, debt payoff/release arrangements, retained lease treatment, material consents, management authority/retention documents, tax-election cooperation and bring-down of the disclosed condition set. No fabricated regulatory order or government certificate substitutes for a jurisdiction assessment.

**Post-close authority.** Nora Ashcombe becomes ARU President/COO; Seth Kettering remains BS&T GM. Fred loses all line authority and performs knowledge transfer only. Existing property CBAs continue. The $500k retention pool and $225k consulting agreement are separate employment/service arrangements, not hidden stock consideration.

**Tax cooperation.** All four sellers and buyer join the intended §338(h)(10) election. Parties use a consistent agreed allocation subject to the source tax model and legal requirements, preserve records, cooperate on returns and allocate seller-period tax obligations explicitly. [Tax memorandum](07_ARU_TAX_STRUCTURE_MEMORANDUM.md).

This summary creates substantive synthetic contract terms for the case. It is not legal advice or an executed agreement between real persons, and it contains no fabricated signatures, tax IDs or official approvals.

The seller group's $49.5M transaction value is $45M direct consideration + $3M escrow + $1.5M excess-cash distribution. The selected January 1–6 economic stub has a winter loss, funded by a separately disclosed seller liquidity contribution to preserve the agreed cash. It does not produce an ordinary profit distribution. This operating-period transfer is separate from share consideration. sections.heading: RED WASH TRANSACTION AND COMMERCIAL INSTRUMENTS
sections.text:
**Classification:** PUBLIC SYNTHETIC DIEGETIC
**Related record:** `SH-PS-RW-TOR-001`

> The instruments below are fictional but are structured to preserve the commercial, legal, environmental, title, regulatory, employee, and source-record issues established in the transaction case. Northstar Minerals, Inc. is the Wyoming corporate seller; Red Wash Mining, LLC is the Wyoming operating company; Pale Sun Inc. is the Delaware buyer/platform.

The transaction sequence and exact July 18, 2025 close are selected canon. Other
day-level instrument dates are synthetic scenario precision unless a controlling
record separately locks one.

---

sections.heading: 1. Mutual Nondisclosure Agreement — October 18, 2024
sections.text:
Parties: Sable Harbor and Northstar Minerals, Inc. (NMI).

Confidential information includes native files and metadata, superseded models, operational knowledge, regulatory correspondence, contracts, financial records, the transaction's existence, and information communicated orally and later identified. No summary or management presentation supersedes the underlying source records. Access is limited to representatives with need to know. Neither party is obligated to transact, and no representation of accuracy arises except in a definitive agreement. Wyoming law governs.

---

sections.heading: 2. Indication of Interest — January 17, 2025
sections.text:
Sable Harbor indicates a preliminary $34 million enterprise/operating value, subject to cash, debt, working capital, ARO, title, permits, contracts, resource, environmental, maintenance, and employee continuity. The indication is nonbinding and explicitly rejects reliance on Northstar's reserve terminology, management projections, or reported EBITDA until verified.

---

sections.heading: 3. Letter of Intent — February 7, 2025
sections.text:
The parties enter a nonbinding LOI at a preliminary $38 million operating value. Binding provisions cover confidentiality, exclusivity, access, publicity, expenses, standstill, and return/destruction. The purchase price remains subject to technical, environmental, title, contract, working-capital, indebtedness, liability, and source-record adjustments. Sable Harbor may walk without fee for a material diligence change.

---

sections.heading: 4. Seller Re-Trade Memorandum — April 11, 2025
sections.text:
Northstar raises its expectation to $48 million after uranium-market improvement and interest from another party. The re-trade does not allocate additional environmental, title, continuity, or resource-model risk. Sable Harbor concludes that a higher price and weaker evidence cannot be reconciled through optimistic assumptions.

---

sections.heading: 5. Sable Harbor Walk-Away Notice — May 5, 2025
sections.text:
Sable Harbor terminates exclusivity and negotiations. The notice identifies no accusation of fraud. It states that the remaining price, environmental, title, continuity, maintenance, contract-consent, resource, and closure uncertainties exceed the approved acquisition envelope. Sable Harbor preserves confidentiality and a possible return path if the allocation of risk changes.

---

sections.heading: 6. Revised Term Sheet — June 6, 2025
7. Equity Purchase Agreement — signed July 2, 2025; closed July 18, 2025
Purchased interests
sections.text: Northstar transfers all equity interests of the dedicated Red Wash operating company. Red Wash remains the holder/operator of the scheduled mine, mill, tailings, equipment, inventory, contracts, permits, records, water interests, easements, and other assets to the extent legally transferable.

sections.heading: Consideration and liabilities
sections.text: Buyer pays $28.0 million cash consideration, with $3.0 million administered through the environmental/title escrow and $0.5 million retained as a holdback under the modeled risk-allocation mechanics. Those amounts are disclosed separately and are not added to consideration a second time. Buyer assumes only scheduled liabilities, including the $16.0 million ARO and $2.5 million other liabilities. Transaction debt and goodwill are zero.

sections.heading: Representations
sections.text:
Seller representations cover organization, authority, capitalization, title, financial statements, absence of undisclosed liabilities, tax, permits, environmental condition, safety, radiation protection, employees, benefits, contracts, customers, suppliers, inventory, mineral interests, systems, data, insurance, litigation, brokers, and source-record completeness.

Resource information is limited to disclosed internal models. Seller does not represent an S-K 1300 reserve statement. The source-record representation includes native files, metadata, model versions, rejected interpretations, and known superseded records.

sections.heading: Covenants
sections.text: Pre-close operation follows ordinary course subject to safety and permit requirements. Seller preserves people, source records, permits, insurance, customers, inventory, and physical condition. No new related-party agreement, unusual inventory sale, permit amendment, or material capital deferral may occur outside the agreed covenant.

sections.heading: Closing deliveries
sections.text: Closing deliveries include equity instruments, officer resignations, disclosure schedules, customer consents, permit-transfer/acceptance evidence, title cures, bill of sale and assignments, escrow, transition-services agreement, employee census, retention agreements, inventory certificate, source-record index, bank/authority changes, and closing certificate.

sections.heading: Indemnity
sections.text:
Indemnity distinguishes fundamental, general, tax, intentional-misrepresentation, title, environmental, and specified known-condition claims. Escrow secures identified title/environmental matters. Fraud and deliberate concealment are not limited by the ordinary cap.

---

sections.heading: 8. Disclosure Schedules
9. Bill of Sale and Assignment
sections.text:
Transfers scheduled mine workings, development, mill, laboratory, tailings equipment, mobile equipment, spares, ore/WIP/product/supply inventory, transferable permits and contracts, books and source files, warranties, site IP, easements, access rights, and water interests. Federal minerals, state licenses, and other nontransferable rights pass only as law permits. Buyer assumes only scheduled liabilities.

---

sections.heading: 10. Environmental and Title Escrow Agreement
sections.text:
A $3.0 million escrow remains for 36 months. It secures predecessor-name easement cure, specified pre-close groundwater and tailings obligations, property/ad-valorem adjustments, and special representation claims. Claims require notice, factual basis, estimated amount, and supporting evidence. Undisputed funds release on schedule. Fraud remedies are not capped by escrow.

---

sections.heading: 11. Transition Services Agreement
sections.text:
Northstar provides up to six months of read-only ERP access, payroll-history support, vendor and contract administration, geological archive extraction, regulatory archive transfer, insurance-claim support, and tax/property-record assistance at cost plus five percent. Northstar receives no post-close operating, safety, product-release, contract, personnel, or capital authority.

---

sections.heading: 12. Cole Retention and Stop-Authority Agreement
sections.text:
Cole remains for an initial three-year term with market cash compensation, retention payments, and Pale Sun profit participation. He may temporarily stop a movement, stope, area, process, or shipment when observed conditions differ materially from the operating basis. He must record the scope, observation, immediate action, and available basis. Review is rapid. sections.heading: Schedule B — clock, free time and service remedies
sections.text:
Tuesday and Friday at 08:00 America/Denver are scheduled Taylor handling windows within the railway's ordinary five-day service. The default limit from interchange receipt to empty release is **72 elapsed hours**, with a **36–48-hour operating goal**; steel has **96 elapsed hours**. Acid and binder target 95% on-time service. UTC elapsed-time arithmetic governs daylight-saving transitions; weekends and clock changes do not disappear from the denominator.

Dispatch uses a weekday exception when the next scheduled window would miss the limit. Where that is insufficient, funded on-call handling begins within 24 elapsed hours, subject to qualified crews and safe movement. Required exception handling is included in the quoted rates and the existing **$48,000 annual fixed allowance**; it creates no new guaranteed fee or hidden revenue. Safety or qualification failure requires a hold and prompt alternate-carrier arrangement, not an unsafe promise to meet a clock.

Free time is 72 elapsed hours from interchange receipt, or 96 for steel. After free time, **customer-caused** occupancy of provider-controlled storage may incur a derived **$50 per car per 24 hours**, prorated hourly. Provider-caused delay earns no storage charge against RWH. This is a synthetic commercial occupancy rate, not an external railroad tariff or statutory amount; baseline finance assumes zero charge because it models no chargeable dwell event.

Each proposed demurrage/storage charge identifies the car, start/end times, free-time expiry, responsible cause, custody source and charging entity. Third-party carrier charges require the actual supporting invoice and the governing carrier rule. The same dwell cost cannot be recovered both as the $50 occupancy charge and a duplicate carrier pass-through. Disputed costs remain identified rather than spread as unexplained intercompany overhead. Provider fault is borne by the responsible provider; customer delay is assigned only on evidence. Shared causes receive a documented allocation, not automatic full billing to the mine.

A provider-caused missed shipment suspends the affected unearned service charge and requires an agreed cure or alternate qualified service. The responsible provider bears reasonable documented incremental replacement cost attributable to its breach, without double recovery. Routine disputes go first to Derek Fenwick/Marta Ellery and the mine receiving lead, then Nora and Mari within five business days. Unresolved commercial disputes proceed through the contract's internal independent review before ordinary legal remedies. A pending dispute never overrides Seth's rail command or Mari/Cole's operating hold.

sections.heading: Schedule C — custody, insurance and qualification
sections.text:
Required event records identify interchange receipt, BS&T dispatch, Taylor spot, unload start, weight/transfer, truck dispatch, mine receipt, empty inspection and empty release. Each retains source time, timezone, operator identity, car/truck/load identifier, weight, seal status where applicable and corrections. An outage uses a signed offline queue and later synchronization preserving both original and corrected timestamps. Reconstructed evidence does not silently replace the original record.

The synthetic ordinary-inbound qualification schedule, effective July 7, records assigned trained handlers, immobilization/transfer procedures, compatible equipment, containment and emergency contacts, approved truck payloads/routes, receiving readiness and stop authority. Internal coverage assumptions are commercial general liability **$2M each occurrence**, motor liability **$2M combined single limit**, and pollution liability **$2M**, with railway protective/contractual coverage reviewed for the specific property. These are derived case contract limits, not universal legal minima, observed insurer quotations or government approvals. The incremental $8,000 insurance budget is a planning allocation within the existing program, not proof that a new stand-alone policy can be bought for that sum. No insurer, policy number or certificate is fabricated.

Each provider bears its own employee, equipment and negligent-performance obligations; RWH bears receiving readiness, customer-directed delay and accurate tender information. Indemnity follows the responsible party's negligent or wrongful conduct and actual supported loss. There is no blanket transfer of mine environmental liabilities, railway legacy claims or ARU acquisition indemnities into this service contract. Fraud, bodily injury, pollution and deliberate safety breaches are not extinguished by a routine service-credit calculation.

Direct uranium-product custody remains **OPEN_GATED**. It requires a separate agreement and evidence of applicable regulatory, route, packaging, customer, equipment, security, insurance, training, emergency and operating qualification. Ordinary acid service is not precedent establishing uranium authority.

sections.heading: Schedule D — assets, billing and termination
sections.text:
RWH owns the **$3.25M** mine receiving/road/storage program. ARU owns **$5.25M** of reusable Taylor infrastructure. The **$8.5M** Phase 1 is separately equity funded; depreciation stays with each owner. The unapproved $6.5M balance of the $15M ceiling is excluded. ARU's separate $11M catch-up and $3.3M sustaining capital are not service consideration or duplicate tariff charges.

Monthly invoices separately identify BS&T rail, ARU terminal and ARU trucking service, actual quantities, source events, accepted rate version and exclusions. Payment is due within 30 calendar days; the model's following-calendar-month settlement may include early payment rather than implying an exact settlement day. December balances remain due in January 2027. Reciprocal seller receivable/revenue and RWH payable/expense share stable invoice IDs. Consolidation eliminates those balances and income/expense once; external costs and capital consumption remain.

A material breach has 30 days to cure after written notice where cure is possible; unsafe or unqualified service may be stopped immediately. Persistent failure, insolvency, loss of essential qualification or uncured material breach permits termination of the affected service. Either party may terminate for convenience after the initial year on 180 days' notice, without a volume penalty or acceleration of unspent capital. Existing supported invoices and accrued cause-assigned charges survive. Each owner retains its assets; termination creates no automatic mine subsidy, purchase option or recovery of every unamortized dollar from the other party.

References: [service plan](../operations/OPERATING_AND_SERVICE_PLAN.md), [rate/capital memorandum](../operations/RATE_AND_CAPITAL_MEMORANDUM.md), [labor/safety controls](../operations/LABOR_SAFETY_AND_CONTROLS.md), [finance source](../source/finance.json) and [authority matrix](../corporate/LEADERSHIP_AND_AUTHORITY.md). sections.heading: Reference editions and availability
sections.text:
Pacific Harbor Line's own [tariff directory](https://www.anacostia.com/resources/for-existing-customers/tariffs/phl/) links PHL 8000-U and PHL 8100-L. Both PDF covers say **issued January 30, 2026; effective January 1, 2026**. The earlier effective date does not establish January 1 publication or company knowledge. This record first observes them on September 5 Pacific time. Their published scope is PHL service in the Los Angeles/Long Beach harbor area, not the fictional Wyoming route.

The source editions are [PHL 8000-U, switching and miscellaneous charges](https://www.anacostia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/2026_Public-Tariff-PHL-8000-U.pdf) and [PHL 8100-L, storage and hazardous-material provisions](https://www.anacostia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/2026_PHL-8100-L-tariff.pdf). Page references below use printed PDF page numbers. They are carrier-published commercial terms, not universal legal requirements.

sections.heading: Comparable units and material differences
sections.text:
| Item | Published carrier reference | Fictional service and inference |
|---|---|---|
| Rail switching | PHL 8000-U item 240, page 5: intra-terminal switching **$654.75 per car** | BS&T ordinary rail components are **$750–$950 per car**. They are $95.25–$295.25, or approximately 14.5%–45.1%, above this reference. The services differ in distance, density and infrastructure; this arithmetic does not establish a justified premium. |
| Dedicated exception capacity | PHL 8000-U item 140, page 3: first eight-hour two-person switching shift **$2,855.47**, including one locomotive/fuel, with **five shifts per week minimum** | Our included exception service and **$48,000 annual fixed allowance** are allocated support for a shared operation, not the purchase of a dedicated crew. They cannot be justified by converting a per-car rate into unlimited exclusive shifts. A sustained exception workload requires recosting. |
| Nonhazardous private-car storage | PHL 8100-L items 8200/8250, page 4: **$68.61 per car-day**, with two credit days and the tariff's calendar-day computation | Our contingent **$50 per car-day** after **72 elapsed hours**, or **96 for steel**, prorates hourly and requires customer causation. It is $18.61/day lower before differences in clocks and credits. No baseline chargeable dwell revenue is assumed. |
| Hazardous-material accessorial | PHL 8100-L item 8700, page 5: private hazardous/residue cars incur **$204.06 per car-day**, no credit days, commencing the day after interchange receipt | This is a separate exposure category. Our internal acid rate/free-time agreement does not waive a real connecting carrier's hazardous-material charges, storage restrictions or demurrage. It also creates no uranium custody permission. |

The first two reference rows are supported by [PHL 8000-U, items 140 and 240](https://www.anacostia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/2026_Public-Tariff-PHL-8000-U.pdf); the last two by [PHL 8100-L, items 8200, 8250, 8350 and 8700](https://www.anacostia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/2026_PHL-8100-L-tariff.pdf). These selected amounts are not a reproduction of the tariffs or a complete estimate of a PHL shipment.

sections.heading: Cost-to-serve and decision
sections.text:
The [operations source](../source/operations.json) remains the case rate authority. Acid is **$950 rail + $700 terminal + four truck trips at $340 = $3,010 per car**. Binder is **$850 + $400 + four trips at $285 = $2,390**. Rail switching references cannot validate unloading equipment, chemical handling or truck cycle costs. The [rate and capital memorandum](../operations/RATE_AND_CAPITAL_MEMORANDUM.md) supplies those separately modeled resources and the 215-car normalized revenue base; its assumptions remain inspectable.

The comparison supports keeping rail, terminal, trucking, exceptional capacity and dwell as separate cost units. It does **not** substantiate the origin Class I linehaul price, chemical terminal price, Wyoming trucking rate, insurance premium or the whole $8.5M capital investment. No identical-route external quote has been obtained or fabricated. Procurement must compare a qualified alternative for the same payload, distance, frequency, equipment, exception coverage and liability allocation before treating the internal price as competitive. If the comparison fails, the agreement allows external service without a minimum-volume penalty.

Controller disposition: retain the current derived rates as the transparent case scenario, retain zero baseline demurrage, and carry external price confirmation as an explicit commercial condition. The $50 contingent rate and 72/96-hour free periods remain negotiated synthetic choices; neither is relabeled a general market norm merely because a carrier publishes a different schedule.

sections.heading: 1. Commercial model
sections.text:
Advisory sells consequential outcomes, decision-grade judgment, implemented capability and durable transfer. It does not sell hours as the primary unit of value.

sections.heading: 2. Matter classes
sections.text: Every contract is assigned one primary commercial class.

sections.heading: A. Measurable Value Matter
sections.text: A financially measurable result can be baselined and attributed with enough rigor to support variable economics.

sections.heading: B. Capability Matter
sections.text: The contracted outcome is a functioning capability state validated through acceptance tests rather than direct financial value.

sections.heading: C. Decision Matter
sections.text: The client is buying independent judgment, investigation, scenario evaluation or decision support where ex-post financial attribution would distort professional independence.

sections.heading: D. Managed Continuity Matter
sections.text:
The client purchases an ongoing operating/service obligation, monitoring, managed analytics, or continuing professional capability.

Hybrid matters are allowed, but each component must be priced and governed explicitly.

sections.heading: 3. Minimum commercial threshold
sections.text:
The normal minimum professional matter fee is **$150,000**, excluding Atlas license, travel, third-party costs, taxes and pass-through expenditures.

Exceptions require a documented strategic, developmental, public-interest, design-partner, or relationship rationale. Small fees are not used to disguise materially larger effort.

sections.heading: 4. Measurable Value Matter pricing
sections.text: The target professional fee is anchored to **verified addressable value**, not total enterprise value or the most optimistic theoretical upside.

sections.heading: Working target bands
sections.text:
| Verified addressable value | Target total fee |
|---:|---:|
| Under $5M | 10–15% |
| $5M–$25M | 7–12% |
| $25M–$100M | 4–8% |
| $100M–$500M | 2–4% |
| Over $500M | 0.5–2.0% |

These are starting disciplines. Complexity, attribution, time-to-value, risk, client dependency, capital intensity, market scarcity and implementation burden can move the quote.

sections.heading: 5. 60/40 structure
sections.text:
The working default for a Measurable Value Matter is:

- **60% committed professional fee**; and
- **40% variable outcome fee**.

The committed portion pays for Sable Harbor accepting the problem, reserving scarce capacity, assuming professional responsibility, operating the Atlas matter environment, and performing the work. The variable portion aligns economics to measured value without making the firm's entire fee hostage to factors outside its control.

The split may move between **40/60 and 80/20** where attribution or client dependency requires. A 100% contingent arrangement is exceptional and requires reserved approval.

Travel and extraordinary third-party expenses are agreed in advance where practical. Ordinary internal compute and routine tooling are part of the firm's cost of delivery unless the contract identifies a separately metered product/service component.

sections.heading: 12. Procurement response

sections.heading: 17. Discounts

Discounts are stated as commercial decisions, not hidden through inflated list price. Accepted reasons include multi-matter commitment, strategic market entry, design partnership, client-provided capability reducing effort, or portfolio economics.

A discount cannot be conditioned on suppressing review, narrowing evidence, predetermined findings, or compromising transfer quality.

sections.heading: 18. Profitability discipline
sections.text:
Finance tracks matter economics using actual internal cost, compute, travel, Atlas consumption, review effort, claims reserve, and collection outcome. A high-value client outcome is not necessarily a profitable matter if delivery was uncontrolled.

The firm studies contribution margin, but professional quality can require spending beyond initial estimates without billing-by-the-hour pressure.

sections.text: The proposal should read as though Sable Harbor knows exactly what it is accountable for. The client should know the problem, success measure, committed price, variable mechanics, Atlas/product charges, dependencies, transfer obligation, and exit path before substantive work begins.

sections.heading: Master agreement RT-MSA-001
sections.text:
Sable Harbor, LLC (SHI), as proposed customer, and the provider legal entity to be
verified in each site order would enter this agreement for facility services.
Switch and IDACORE are selected provider brands; neither brand alone establishes
the contracting subsidiary. No signature, incorporation number or provider
acknowledgment is represented. Each party acts only in its own legal capacity.

The provider would supply assigned enclosure space, metered power, cooling within
the accepted equipment envelope, building access, facility operation and scoped
remote hands. Sable Harbor retains equipment title, workloads, network boundaries,
identity administration, keys, data, application operations, backup policy,
classification, customer commitments and institutional authority. Facility access
does not authorize logical access or transfer J2's information authority.

An executed order would identify the building, enclosure, delivery points, power
and cooling configuration, measurement method and commercial lines. An order
would commence billing only after technical acceptance, except explicitly agreed
reservation charges. A purchase order cannot override this agreement. Precedence
would be: signed negotiated deviations identifying the affected clause; site order
for quantities/dates/price; this master; security and evidence schedules; other
incorporated schedules. A weaker order protection requires an express deviation
accepted by Legal and the accountable risk owner. Provider website changes would
not amend the agreement.

The proposed initial term is 12 months after acceptance for Boise and 24 months
for Reno, each subject to negotiation. Renewal would be by written agreement or
an expressly selected renewal mechanism with 90-day notice; no automatic extension
is assumed in finance. Material breach would allow written notice and 30 days to
cure where curable. An imminent security or safety incident requires immediate
containment coordination. Termination does not transfer customer property, keys
or confidential data and does not extinguish preservation duties.

sections.heading: Site order RT-SO-RENO, revision 1.0.0
sections.text:
Customer: Sable Harbor, LLC. Selected provider/campus: Switch TAHOE RENO — The
Citadel Campus. Provider legal party, building, enclosure and commencement date:
unverified/unassigned. State: draft, procurement pending; zero reserved capacity.

Request 75 and 100 kW alternatives, expansion to 200–250 kW, dedicated controlled
enclosure, A/B delivery each capable of carrying the accepted load, two diverse
carrier entrances and 10 Gbps initial transport with 100 Gbps pathway. Power is
usable IT delivery, not summed redundant PSU ratings. High-density and future
liquid-cooling compatibility require provider confirmation; no campus-wide
marketing specification establishes this enclosure's capability.

The financial sensitivity uses $350/kW/month as an analyst assumption, not a Switch
quote, plus separately modeled connectivity and remote hands. Installation,
deposits, taxes, cabinet fees, expansion reservations and cancellation exposures
require itemized quotations before execution. An assumed commitment in the cost
model is not a commitment to Switch. The service order incorporates every schedule
below. Finance and Procurement approve commercial completeness; Legal approves the
legal party and negotiated instrument; Technology and Security accept delivery.

sections.heading: Site order RT-SO-BOISE, revision 1.0.0
sections.text:
Customer: Sable Harbor, LLC. Selected facility: IDACORE Boise, 2653 S Victory View
Way, Boise, Idaho 83709. Legal party, enclosure, commencement and actual capacity
remain unverified/unassigned. State: draft, procurement pending.

The provisional recovery envelope is 25 kW with 50 and 100 kW expansion cases.
The previous unexplained 6 kW lower bound is superseded for this design. The base
2027 configuration estimates 23.6 kW peak and 14.6 kW synthetic typical draw;
later scenarios exceed 25 kW. No recovery objective is verified by these estimates.

Public pricing reports $300/kW/month, power included and actual-draw billing.
At 14.6 kW synthetic average this is $4,380/month before separate connectivity,
remote hands, taxes and other quoted lines. A hypothetical 25 kW committed case
would be $7,500/month; that is a sensitivity, not the public billing rule. Meter
interval, averaging, demand peaks, minimums and settlement must be specified in the
accepted order. The pricing page's short-term wording and 12-month FAQ require
explicit resolution. No cooling/power claims from IDACORE East are imported here.

sections.heading: Schedule A — Commercial measurement and invoices
sections.text:
Every price line would identify currency, tax treatment, quantity, unit, included
service, rate source, escalation, start/stop dates and billing basis. The accepted
schedule must separately show cage/cabinet, metered or committed usable power,
cooling surcharge, setup, cross-connect, IP transit, private transport, OOB, remote
hands, receiving/storage, refundable deposit, prepayment, expansion option,
cancellation, de-installation and migration overlap. A zero line must explicitly
mean included or waived; blank means unquoted. A/B redundancy is not twice the
productive load. Power-inclusive rates cannot receive a second utility/PUE charge.

Meters would expose interval data and calibration records. An invoice would show
meter identifiers, interval completeness, actual draw, peak, committed quantity
if applicable, power factor where material and calculation. Customer may dispute
a supported discrepancy within 60 days, pay undisputed amounts, and request joint
re-performance. The parties would resolve meter failure through an agreed estimate
with disclosed dates; missing readings cannot silently become measured evidence.
Annual escalation requires a stated percentage/cap and anniversary; no unstated
pass-through or auto-reservation is approved.

sections.heading: Schedule B — Availability and credits
sections.text:
Proposed critical-power target: 100% at each agreed customer delivery point under
the accepted usable load. An outage begins at first loss of required delivery and
ends at restored stable delivery documented by telemetry. Count intervals once
per affected service. A/B loss with surviving load is a redundancy incident even
when no qualifying outage occurs. Power, network and application availability
are measured separately; this schedule promises no application uptime.

Monthly availability equals (eligible minutes minus qualifying unavailable
minutes) / eligible minutes. Calculate each affected enclosure/service before
aggregation; unrelated healthy cabinets cannot dilute a failed enclosure. Agreed
maintenance exclusions would require the notice and approval record, precise
interval and reason. Emergency maintenance and force-majeure exclusions remain
visible in gross outage and risk reports even when excluded from credits.

Customer-proposed credits against affected monthly recurring facility charges:
any qualifying interruption with availability at least 99.9%: 5%; below 99.9% to
99%: 10%; below 99% to 95%: 25%; below 95%: 50%. Credit capped at 50% of that base;
taxes, unrelated services and one-time installation are excluded. A 60-minute
qualifying outage in 43,200 minutes yields 99.8611% and $1,000 on a $10,000 affected
base. No outage yields zero credit. Claims would be submitted within 60 days with
provider reconciliation; proposed automatic crediting remains a negotiation item.
Three qualifying breaches in a rolling six months would permit termination of the
affected order without early termination fees. Credits never establish acceptable
risk or substitute for corrective action.

sections.heading: Schedule C — Remote hands, incidents and maintenance
sections.text:
P1 remote hands: acknowledgment within 15 minutes and qualified engagement within
30 minutes. Record ticket receipt, acknowledgment, dispatch, physical arrival,
hands-on start, restoration and closure separately. Engagement is not restoration.
Customer-caused stop clocks require a timestamped request and customer concurrence;
provider staffing shortages do not automatically stop the clock.

For qualifying availability P1s, initial notice would be within 30 minutes of
detection or reasonable awareness. Suspected or confirmed security impact would
be notified within one hour; confirmation cannot defer preliminary notice.
Use the agreed secure incident channel, scope/time/known-impact statement,
preservation action and next update time. Provide hourly P1 updates until stable,
initial cause analysis within five business days and a corrective-action plan
within ten, with uncertainty stated. Provider does not speak for customer to
regulators or clients without authority.

Ordinary planned maintenance requires 14 days notice; material electrical/network
work requires 30 where feasible. Describe affected delivery, redundancy loss,
qualified personnel, rollback, test plan and escalation. Emergency work prioritizes
safety and prompt notice, followed by retrospective review. Tenant personnel must
not pull live facility feeds or operate provider switchgear. Electrical tests require
provider approval, qualified operators and a written safety/rollback plan.

sections.heading: Schedule D — Physical and logical security
sections.text:
Provider would maintain controlled perimeter, staffed/monitored entry, visitor
identity and escorts, anti-tailgating measures, alarm response, synchronized CCTV
and access logs. Customer supplies its named access list, role/purpose and expiry.
Provider would promptly execute authorized revocations and preserve the timestamp.
Quarterly reviews reconcile all approved people, provider master-access users,
visitors, expired contractors and emergency entries. Emergency access is logged,
bounded and retrospectively reviewed; it is not routine privileged access.

Remote hands requires an authenticated customer work order, asset identifiers,
permitted steps, maintenance window and explicit prohibition on data/key access.
Receiving uses chain of custody, package inspection, quarantine and inventory
reconciliation. Lost seals, serial mismatches or unauthorized work stop acceptance
and escalate. Provider facility management networks remain outside customer trust;
customer controls edge, OOB, identities, HSMs, segmentation and cryptographic policy.

sections.heading: Schedule E — Confidentiality, records and assurance
sections.text:
Each party would use confidential information only for the contracted purpose,
restrict access to authorized personnel, protect transmission and storage, and
notify compelled disclosure where lawful. No model training, private-data reuse or
cross-customer sharing is granted. Equipment custody does not grant a data license.
Provider-held records follow agreed class-based retention, legal holds and secure
return/deletion; this is not a blanket retention period for Alexandria Canon.

Requested control evidence would be delivered within ten business days, subject to
documented lawful/confidentiality restrictions and agreed alternative evidence.
Monthly packs include incident populations, maintenance, access anomalies, metering,
capacity and credits. Annual assurance review requests report scope, auditor,
period, opinion, exceptions, subservice treatment and CUECs; absence stays an open
evidence dependency. A bridge letter is management representation, not an auditor
extension of the tested period. Secure reports must not enter this public repo.

sections.heading: Schedule F — Continuity, concentration, title and exit
sections.text:
Provider would disclose material subcontracted facility services and changes that
affect agreed controls, concentration or recovery. Customer approval/escalation
would apply to material adverse changes under the negotiated order. Lists of
carriers or distinct provider brands do not establish route, identity or key
independence. Annual integrated DR and risk-based component tests require agreed
scope, prerequisites, recovery point, integrity checks and failback reconciliation.

Customer retains title to hardware, media, data and keys. Proposed terms prohibit
liens or access restrictions that prevent emergency recovery or orderly removal;
Legal must resolve actual enforceability and provider deviations. Exit would allow
90 days coordinated transition, continued paid service at agreed rates, inventory
and media custody, secure shipping, cross-connect cessation, access revocation,
retained evidence and final billing reconciliation. Keys are never surrendered as
an exit condition. Deletion confirmation identifies records, method, scope and
legal-hold exceptions rather than asserting deletion of held material.

sections.heading: Schedule G — Liability, insurance and approval register
sections.text:
Proposed ordinary direct-damage cap is 12 months of affected fees; confidentiality,
unauthorized property disposal, intentional misconduct and gross negligence require
separate negotiated treatment. No enforceability opinion is supplied. Customer
requests provider general liability, cyber and property/custody coverage with
limits tied to equipment exposure; certificates, exclusions and cancellation
notice remain unreceived. Customer insures its equipment as separately arranged.
No indemnity, consequential-loss waiver or subrogation term is treated as accepted.

Negotiation register: legal counterparty verification (Legal); price/meter/minimum
and deposits (Finance/Procurement); rack/cooling/A-B/route acceptance (Technology);
access and evidence rights (Security); liability/lien/insurance terms (Legal);
recovery and exit (Reliability). All are OPEN FOR NEGOTIATION, not provider-choice
questions. Incompatible mandatory terms require owner disposition, not substitution.

sections.heading: Commercial operations and contract economics
sections.text:
Status: implemented conditional planning histories. All customer decisions,
approvals, incidents and future dates are public synthetic assumptions for
2027–2031. They are not operating records or executed agreements.

The successor retains the accepted business model's 75 contract sources and
three scenarios. `source/commercial.json` supplies additional events; it never
rewrites baseline contract values. Annual subscriptions remain prepaid billed
terms, recognized monthly when service occurs. Deployment fees remain separate
accepted work. Atlas licenses remain product revenue, with its outcome delivery
capacity reserved separately from its commercial service pool.

sections.heading: Pipeline, capacity and service
sections.text:
Every eligible contract produces dated pipeline evidence until activation. The
default synthetic outcome is won on its original start date. Explicit overrides
exercise lost opportunities, permanently held opportunities, and decisions
delayed beyond the planned start. A won opportunity still needs the scenario's
acceptance delay and available deployment capacity; neither a planned start nor
a customer decision bypasses capacity.

Each product unit dedicates 20% of its workforce-derived delivery capacity to one
shared monthly service pool. Opening customers reserve routine support first,
incident work consumes the remainder next, and deployments use what remains.
Newly activated customers also reserve their current month's support. Individual
support tickets, incident movements and deployment acceptance records support
the capacity rollforward. No hour in this pool is allocated twice. Opening
customer support reservations include that month's renewal/exit administration;
they may therefore remain for a customer whose service ends during the month.
Routine unmet monthly demand is reported as backlog for that service month;
incident remediation hours carry forward until resolved.

Incident demand is an explicit source assumption. Failure to finish that month's
incident demand records a service breach, creates a single earned-service credit,
and enters the contract's renewal review. A breach in the preceding 12 months
causes modeled nonrenewal at the configured threshold. Resolving the incident
does not erase the original breach. Increasing service capacity can avoid the
breach, its credit and the later customer loss. The original scenario churn rule
remains as a separately identified renewal cause.

These are monthly planning mechanics, not a claim that support hours establish
production uptime or a particular contractual SLA. The model grants no live
customer entitlement and does not choose a deployment/runtime architecture.

sections.heading: Versions, amendments and customer credits
sections.text:
Activation, renewal, expansion, price amendments, contraction and cancellation
create immutable version rows. Each retains its applied month, original
effective month and synthetic approval identifier. A change that becomes due
before delayed activation is held and retried; it is applied once after actual
activation. A change for a lost or closed customer receives an explicit
nonapplicable disposition. Delays do not silently erase amendments.

Positive changes bill the additional monthly rate for the unexpired part of the
existing annual term. Contractions credit the unearned portion of the same
term. Cancellation credits the entire unearned balance, ends recurring revenue,
and prevents future service recognition. Amendments change seats and actual
monthly recognized revenue as well as the reported ARR. Annual renewal
escalation applies to the effective rate, including earlier changes.

Each billed invoice retains an unearned claim. Recognition consumes claims in
order; reductions consume remaining claims from newest to oldest. Earned-service
credits use earned invoice capacity and cannot consume the unearned balance.
The credit module applies credits to open AR, surviving written-off claims, and
only then refundable collected cash. Commercial code does not bypass those
collection, credit or refund controls.

sections.heading: Reconciliations and review tables
sections.text:
| Table | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `commercial_pipeline` | Customer decision, planned activation and capacity/acceptance holds |
| `contract_versions` | Effective rate, seats, term and approval history |
| `commercial_changes` | Applied, held or nonapplicable amendment disposition |
| `commercial_service_tickets` | Monthly routine support demand and service |
| `service_incidents` | Incident demand, work performed, open hours and preserved breach |
| `commercial_renewals` | Renewal decision and service/scenario cause |
| `commercial_capacity` | Shared capacity, support, incident, deployment and unused hours |
| `commercial_metrics` | Active customers, concentration, ARR and support backlog |
| `commercial_arr_bridge` | Opening + new + expansion + price − contraction − churn = closing ARR |
| `commercial_deferred_rollforward` | Opening + billings − unearned credits − recognition = closing deferred revenue |

All scenarios cover every month. Every baseline contract has a deferred
rollforward, including zero balances before activation and after closure. These
balances reconcile to invoice claims and the product unit's general ledger.
Earned-service credits reduce revenue through credit-note journals; they do not
reduce gross contractual ARR or deferred revenue a second time.

Validation independently checks complete, unique monthly populations, continuous
opening/closing balances, aggregate ARR, deferred balances against month-end
books, capacity allocation, approval timing and nonnegative balances. Tests also
exercise changes in capacity, lost opportunities, delayed amendments, actual
invoices and journal consequences, cancellation, and deliberately corrupted
exported bridges.

**Version:** 0.1.0 · **Planning horizon:** 2027–2031 · **PR:** #112  
**State:** Implemented planning model. Owner-approved sourcing direction is pending canonical acceptance; numerical requirements and prices are proposals, not approved operating facts.

This package turns the September 9 decisions into a populated service inventory, shared-resource and supplier-dependency records, and an executable cost/capacity/staffing comparison. It does not deploy infrastructure, purchase anything, alter payroll, or rewrite existing finance releases.

sections.heading: Registers and inputs
sections.text:
| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| [Service register](source/services.json) | 57 service records, actual work, accountable roles, business recipients, sourcing, linked support, dependencies and CCF controls. |
| [Internal support register](source/components.json) | 49 teams/functions, facilities and environments. Design requirements are separated from existing functions and unknown occupied capacity. |
| [External counterparty/dependency register](source/counterparties.json) | Four source-named parties and 49 service-dependency requirements. Unselected suppliers remain null; internal ARU-to-Red Wash service is separately identified. |
| [Workload and recovery requirements](source/workloads.json) | All six hosting classes; proposed demand, recovery targets, dependency order and failure-domain tests. |
| [Economics and transition inputs](source/economics.json) | Explicit synthetic rates, workloads, seat mix, staff-effort assumptions, asset lives, alternatives, sensitivities, exclusions and staged ownership gates. |
| [Source inventory and finance extract](source/provenance.json) | Reviewed main/PR revisions, source paths/blob checks, states and the conditional finance-policy extract. |

The service and dependency files use `columns` plus row arrays to keep diffs manageable. Their common defaults are explicit in the same files. The loader expands every field and generates ordinary JSON and CSV registers. `null` means unknown/not approved, not zero or not applicable. Source definitions, expanded exports and database tables have distinct roles; editing generated exports does not change inputs.

sections.heading: Run
sections.text:
Python 3.11 or newer; the service model itself uses only the standard library. Run from the repository root:

```bash
python -m enterprise.services.model validate --repository-root .
python -m unittest discover -s enterprise/services/tests -v
python -m enterprise.services.model build --repository-root . --output /tmp/sable-services-run --database
```

Use a fresh output directory when requesting SQLite: the builder refuses to silently replace an existing database. Omit `--repository-root` only for isolated model tests; that mode does not claim to have checked repository source bytes or CCF/site references.

Outputs include expanded registers, monthly costs, staffing/allocations, SaaS cost lines, capacity, a finance bridge, comparison CSV/JSON, 45 demand/price sensitivity results, a readable report, a checksum manifest and optional SQLite with foreign-key-enforced service/component/dependency links. The manifest excludes SQLite bytes because database packaging is not a canonical identity; source and tabular outputs provide reproducibility.

Example local query:

```sql
SELECT s.name, s.sourcing, d.id, d.provider_id
FROM service AS s
JOIN service_dependency AS sd ON sd.service_id=s.id
JOIN dependency AS d ON d.id=sd.dependency_id
WHERE d.provider_id IS NULL
ORDER BY s.name, d.id;
```

sections.heading: Comparison scope
sections.text:
Four architecture alternatives use the same logical service demand: cloud-heavy transition; mixed cloud/owned colocation; owned baseline in professional colocation; and eventual owned primary physical plant with independent recovery still in colocation. Every alternative preserves internally controlled restricted infrastructure and local equipment. A fifth scenario models an illustrative transition at months 7 and 19. Those months are analytical assumptions, not promised installation dates; the recorded acceptance gates control execution.

Prices are analyst-entered synthetic comparison assumptions, **not researched tariffs, vendor quotes or commitments**. Headcount, demand, growth, license mix, workload effort and numerical recovery targets must be validated before procurement or staffing approval. No preferred architecture is declared cheapest in the real world from this illustrative model.

The [generated comparison](generated/comparison.csv) and [report](generated/REPORT.md) are reproducible examples, not new canon. The full outputs are generated by the CI workflow and attached to its run as build artifacts, not represented as a controlled release package.

sections.heading: Accounting and workforce safeguards
sections.text:
The existing 2027 conditional policy retains 48 occupied / 54 authorized ESS positions. Its $216,000 annual vendor allowance, $1,140,000 annual corporate facilities allowance and $6,720,000 ESS payroll are displayed in the bridge. They are **not automatically deducted** from the new model. Actual reused staff, mapped overlap and generated product-compute expense require source-level reconciliation before a net successor forecast can be accepted.

The model reads contract input exposure separately and labels it before churn/renewal/engine adjustments. That exposure is not booked compute expense and is not used as a replacement credit. Original policy, assets, industrial books, released forecasts and intercompany eliminations are not rewritten.

Shared team costs are counted once and allocated across workloads. Required fractional capacity, rounded dedicated positions, reusable staff, contractors and approved hiring are distinct. A hypothetical reuse scenario is not evidence of available people. J2/Atlas personnel are not treated as a spare platform workforce. Education billets are not added to J2 a second time.

Capital cash, operating cash, depreciation, net book value, refresh and exit costs are separate. Depreciation starts the month after purchase; refresh is not simultaneously expensed as a reserve. Owned physical plant is capacity-bounded and has a separate useful life and facilities workforce.

sections.heading: Boundaries and next acceptance gates
sections.text:
Read [operating assumptions and acceptance gates](docs/OPERATING_ASSUMPTIONS_AND_GATES.md) before interpreting targets or totals. Particularly important: the local hardware envelope is not a complete resilient OT design; N+1 CPU calculations do not prove storage/GPU redundancy, carrier independence or RTO/RPO; SaaS availability does not establish a customer-controlled recoverable runtime; and immutable online and offline backup controls require separate evidence.

Authority remains with the [sourcing decision record](../../docs/canon/THIRD_PARTY_SERVICES_SOURCING_DECISIONS_2026-09-09.md), its [scope supplement](../../docs/canon/THIRD_PARTY_SERVICES_IMPLEMENTATION_SCOPE_2026-09-09.md), and accepted Technology/ESS/J2/business doctrine. PR acceptance is distinct from implementing or funding an operating estate.

It updates selected counterparties and planned placements, emits `runtime.json`, and joins the separate enterprise finance and geography successors. sections.heading: Purpose
sections.text: This doctrine keeps authority close to accountable competence while ensuring exposures capable of changing or contaminating the enterprise receive the right attention. It is not a spending-approval ladder. Authority follows exposure, accountability, knowledge, and demonstrated judgment; title alone does not determine latitude.

sections.heading: Band 1 — management
sections.text: Management operates without repeated permission inside approved strategy, budget, and exposure envelope. Experimentation in that envelope is presumed permissible. Two similarly titled leaders may have different latitude where competence, operating record, or exposure differs. A bounded experiment can be large in dollars and remain delegated when its consequence is genuinely capped.

sections.heading: Band 2 — board-reserved
sections.text: Board reservation ordinarily includes annual strategy and budget; material unplanned commitments; material debt, guarantees, or security; creation of legal entities; material related-party matters; consequential but nonexistential M&A; senior executive appointment/removal; and major departure from approved operating plans. The list describes consequence classes, not a device for converting every decision into board administration.

sections.heading: Band 3 — transformational
sections.text:
Transformational matters can change what Sable Harbor is rather than merely what it owns or how it operates. Examples are sale or change of control; entry into a genuinely new regulated domain or asset class; enterprise-threatening leverage; fundamental restructuring; and existential strategic bets.

The cultural target is broad support roughly equivalent to five of nine directors for ordinary reserved matters and six of nine for transformational matters. These are deliberative norms, not mathematical legal vetoes or investor protections.

sections.heading: Exposure over spend
sections.text: Escalation responds to irreversibility, external propagation, catastrophic potential, legal/regulatory exposure, environmental/community exposure, safety consequence, and uncontrolled enterprise exposure. A small action with an uncapped safety, environmental, or legal tail may escalate at once. A larger but genuinely capped financial trial may not.

sections.heading: Anti-circumvention
sections.text: Economically or operationally related commitments are considered together. A decision may not be split by invoice, phase, entity, counterparty, timing, or nominal workstream to evade an approval boundary. Discovery that a series forms one exposure triggers reassessment; it does not automatically imply misconduct where aggregation was not reasonably knowable.

sections.heading: Subsidiary right to be wrong
sections.text:
ARU, BS&T, and the dedicated Red Wash operator retain delegated judgment inside their envelopes. Corporate preference, status, or hindsight is insufficient to seize a decision. Corporate intervention identifies a real enterprise contagion path, such as parent guarantee, shared scarce capacity, shared liability, enterprise reputation/regulatory effect, cross-business dependency, or common capital exposure.

If no path exists, the accountable subsidiary may make a decision corporate would not choose. Corporate can challenge, request evidence, change a future envelope through proper governance, or learn afterward; it cannot manufacture contagion to win an ordinary disagreement.

sections.heading: Decision record
sections.text: Escalation records the decision, accountable owner, applicable envelope, identified exposure, aggregation analysis, requested decision body, material assumptions/unknowns, dissent, and later disposition. The record preserves who owned the judgment at the time.

sections.heading: Enterprise Support Services
Chief of ESS
sections.text:
The **Chief of ESS** is the administrative head of the umbrella, not the substantive superior of every corporate officer housed within it. The role coordinates shared administration, budget mechanics, facilities, staffing support, service quality, and cross-functional coherence.

Membership in ESS does **not** imply that the CFO, General Counsel, senior People & Culture leader, technology leader, CISO, or other substantive officer loses direct standing with the CEO or Board where the office's responsibilities require it. The Chief of ESS cannot convert administrative coordination into generalized approval authority.

sections.heading: Substantive reporting and professional lines
sections.text:
The General Counsel has direct standing with the Chief Executive Officer and Board when professional duties require it. OGC owns legal advice and Corporate Secretary mechanics; it does not become a substitute management chain.

Risk & Compliance is a combined management challenge/co-ordination function. Management owns risks and controls. Risk & Compliance builds compliance architecture, risk visibility, policy/control co-ordination, CCF stewardship, and escalation, but does not acquire ordinary operating authority.

Finance owns authoritative financial truth and enterprise financial standards while remaining bounded on business judgment as defined in controlling corporate doctrine.

People & Culture owns the enterprise people-system profession and employee experience; it does not own every manager's human responsibilities.

Technology Services owns shared technology capability and platforms while product/business engineering remains with the businesses.

The CISO maintains an independent security authority boundary proportionate to material security obligations and does not become a generalized veto office.

sections.heading: Internal Audit independence
sections.text:
Internal Audit is structurally separate from OGC, Risk & Compliance, Finance, Technology Services, J2, and management control ownership. Internal Audit reports **functionally to the Board Audit & Compliance Committee**. Administrative matters may flow through the CEO/ESS environment only where they do not impair audit independence.

No ESS leader may suppress, pre-clear, edit for convenience, or condition an Internal Audit communication to the Audit & Compliance Committee. Internal Audit controls audit scope, methods, findings, and communications subject to its charter and committee oversight.

sections.heading: Independence doctrine
sections.text:
Sable Harbor preserves separate challenge mechanisms because combining them would weaken all of them.

1. **Management owns the business and its risks.** Operating leaders own controls, remediation, performance, and risk inside delegated authority.
2. **OGC advises lawfully.** Legal identifies legal boundaries and lawful paths without substituting for management judgment.
3. **Risk & Compliance challenges and co-ordinates.** It does not become the enterprise decision-maker.
4. **Finance states financial truth.** Financial authority does not silently become operating command.
5. **Internal Audit independently evaluates.** It does not own the activities it audits.
6. **J2 remains separate.** J2 establishes Contact, forms Judgment, provides Orientation, and supports learning. It is not Internal Audit, Compliance, Legal, Finance, Security, or Risk.

Internal Audit may audit J2 or ESS processes when within scope. J2 may surface facts or uncertainty relevant to Internal Audit. Neither supervises the other.

sections.heading: Physical design
sections.text:
ESS functions may share buildings and service infrastructure for administrative efficiency. Internal Audit should remain physically distinct—such as a separate secured floor/suite—even where located in the same headquarters complex.

J2 is physically separate from ESS. Future Sacramento headquarters floor plans must preserve these distinctions while allowing ordinary collaboration.

sections.heading: Anti-empire rule
sections.text:
ESS exists to support the enterprise. It may not convert legal review, compliance/risk work, finance, people services, technology, security, procurement, safety, quality, or administrative convenience into generalized approval rights over ordinary business decisions unless a specific law, board-reserved matter, policy, or delegated authority expressly requires it.

The governing principle is: **challenge and support must be strong; authority must remain explicit.**

sections.text: OGC is deliberately traditional and restrained. Legal advises; management decides. Legal may state when the law forecloses an action, but it is not a substitute management layer. sections.heading: 5. Finance doctrine
sections.text:
Finance is intentionally formidable: **imperial over financial truth, bounded on business judgment.**

Finance owns authoritative economic records, common financial language, treasury, enterprise financial standards, capital visibility, and the integrity of financial representations. It may challenge unsupported economics and require financial truth to be stated faithfully. It does not gain authority to run a business merely because it can measure it. Business judgment remains with the appropriate accountable owner.

No-use-it-or-lose-it budgeting. Returning unused capital is evidence of judgment, not failure.

sections.heading: 6. People & Culture constitution
sections.text: People & Culture exists to make Sable Harbor an exceptional place for exceptional people to do serious work over a long career. **Continuity is capital.** The function is judged by whether capability, judgment, relationships, and experience compound rather than constantly being discarded.

sections.heading: People operations — invisible excellence
Benefit-friction principle
sections.text:
Never give with one hand and take with the other. Every benefit is evaluated for employee cost in money, time, hassle, or stigma. A benefit nullified by friction is a design defect. This applies at the lived level of the least senior employee, not merely from a manager's perspective.

Examples of the doctrine include free on-premise parking where driving is a normal means of reaching the office, meaningful transit support where useful, and eliminating administrative costs that cancel the value of an offered benefit.

sections.heading: Hybrid work
sections.text: **Work where the work works best.** Sable Harbor is genuinely hybrid where the role permits it. There is no arbitrary office-day quota as a substitute for judgment. Employees are expected to know when the work benefits from physical presence: collaboration, mentoring, difficult coordination, or material human interaction. The office must earn the commute through useful spaces, excellent team environments, and real culture rather than forced fun or perk theater.
